st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value

It also provides a concrete implementation model based on continuous experimentation, pilots, team-level champions, shared use cases and organisational support, while offering no measured productivity or quality outcomes.

kp.k: Repsol distinguishes usage volume from innovative AI practice
kp.d: In this Harvey company-blog interview, Repsol legal counsel Javier Díez Tomillo distinguishes quantitative power users, identified through queries and usage, from qualitative power users, identified through output quality and exploration of new uses. He reports tracking about 30 power users among 150 legal-team users, with about six or seven meeting both definitions. These are his descriptions of internal adoption, not findings from an independent evaluation.
qs: The quantitative ones are the top users in terms of queries and usage, they're power users because they're more familiar with the tool.
Then we have the qualitative ones, people who are using Harvey less frequently, but what they're doing has better output, better quality, or they're pushing the frontier of what's possible.
Out of 150 users in our legal team, we're following about 30 power users, and about six or seven satisfy both definitions.

kp.d: Díez Tomillo defines advanced AI practice as continually discovering use cases and improving how colleagues use AI, rather than retaining a previously sophisticated workflow. Repsol's Harvey Taskforce institutionalizes this activity through power users and champions participating in pilots and testing.
qs: For me, the power user is the person who is constantly finding new use cases, who is making us use AI better because they are pushing Harvey.
If you found a sophisticated way of using Harvey one year ago and you're not improving on that, then for me you're not a top user.
We have a group that participates in all the pilots and testing, called the “Harvey Taskforce”, a group of power users and champions that are leading the change.

kp.k: Technical fluency and workload reportedly encourage advanced adoption
kp.d: Díez Tomillo identifies youth, technical fluency and heavy workloads as traits his team observes among power users. He tentatively relates youth to less entrenched working habits and argues that heavy workloads incentivize technological mastery and innovative use. These are practitioner observations; the interview supplies no statistical test or causal study.
qs: First, being younger, which may be the converse of having long-established ways of working.
Second, being tech-savvy, and having that ease with programming and technology.
Third, having a heavy workload, for obvious reasons, this incentivizes people to master the technology. They're also more likely to be innovative in the way they use it.

kp.k: Prior digital transformation provided foundations for AI adoption
kp.d: Díez Tomillo credits a legal-department transformation project launched three years before the interview with preparing Repsol for AI. Its focus included technology, knowledge management, internal communication and digital training, with an innovation mindset presented as an important enabling condition.
qs: Three years ago, we launched a big transformation project across the legal department on technology, knowledge management, and how we communicate that internally.
A big part was creating an innovation mindset.
We pushed hard on digital training, a foundation that helped enormously when AI arrived.

kp.k: Peer champions and shared use cases spread adoption
kp.d: Díez Tomillo describes a platform for sharing discovered use cases and efforts to identify a top user on each team. He argues that informal peer interaction spreads adoption more effectively than formal meetings, presenting this as Repsol's practical approach to cultivating innovation rather than a measured comparison of training methods.
qs: We also created a platform where people can share use cases they've discovered.
And we try to find a "top user" on each team who can spread adoption organically.
The best evangelism happens over coffee, not in formal meetings.

kp.k: Corporate infrastructure supports legal AI implementation
kp.d: Díez Tomillo reports that company-wide prioritization of AI, including creation of a GenAI Centre, supports legal-team adoption. IT and other corporate functions assist with process mapping, ROI calculation and training; the interview does not report calculated ROI results.
qs: We are also very lucky as the company is prioritizing AI implementation, including the creation of a GenAI Centre.
We have the support of the IT team and other corporate areas that help us leverage AI such as mapping processes, calculating ROI, and training.

kp.k: Experimentation challenges lawyers' fear of failure
kp.d: Díez Tomillo recommends open-ended play to learn technology and reduce lawyers' reluctance to undertake activities without assured successful completion. He also recommends understanding basic technological concepts to design workflows and learning what not to do. His assertion that Harvey is secure and experimentation risks only time is his own characterization, not a security finding presented in the interview.
qs: Something we're trying to change is to help lawyers lose the fear of failure.
For lawyers, it's like "if I start something I need to end it well," but I think the best way to learn how to use technology is to play: don't try to get anything specific, just see what you can do.
Harvey is a secure environment, so the worst thing you can lose is time.
Sometimes knowing what not to do is more useful than knowing what to do.
You need to understand how the technology works at a basic level, and understand the concepts, so you can design workflows accordingly.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Díez Tomillo describes AI adoption as a continuing change in in-house legal working practices, driven by experimentation, peer champions and organisational support rather than usage volume alone.
pts.d: Javier Díez Tomillo, Legal Counsel, New Law and Digital at Repsol, distinguishes frequent Harvey users from users who achieve better-quality output or discover new applications; he regards continual improvement and exploration as central to power use. He reports that younger age, technological fluency and heavy workloads are associated with power use, suggesting that established working habits can inhibit adoption and workload pressure incentivises mastery and innovation. He credits prior digital training, an innovation mindset, shared use cases, team-level champions and informal exchanges with supporting adoption. Corporate prioritisation, a GenAI Centre and IT support provide process mapping, ROI calculation and training. He recommends low-stakes experimentation and basic technological understanding to help lawyers overcome fear of failure and design workflows. His description of Harvey as secure is a speaker assertion, not a documented security assessment. Separately, the Harvey Team's closing editorial framing characterises leading practitioners as achieving 'transformational results'; the interview does not specify quantified service-delivery results. Neither speaker nor publisher makes a concrete forecast about lawyer displacement, prices or legal-market restructuring.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of Díez Tomillo's first-hand implementation experience, descriptive internal user counts and qualitative observations at Repsol.
pts.d: Díez Tomillo reports organising Harvey's pilot, evaluation and rollout and participating in betas and pilots with a colleague. Among 150 legal-team users, Repsol follows approximately 30 power users, with six or seven meeting both quantitative and qualitative definitions. A 'Harvey Taskforce' participates in pilots and testing. These counts describe adoption and internal user classifications; they are not measured productivity or quality improvements. The interview supplies no comparative output assessment, time-saving figures, realised ROI, demographic analysis or causal test of the claimed adoption drivers. ROI calculation is mentioned as an area of corporate support, without results. The publisher presents the interview as part of research into power users and links to an RSGI feature, but the supplied document contains no findings or methodology from that feature.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern adoption as reported in March 2026, supported by a transformation initiative begun three years earlier; sustained power use requires ongoing learning.
pts.d: The interview was published on March 30, 2026. Díez Tomillo dates the legal department's wider technology, knowledge-management and internal-communication transformation to 'three years ago', approximately 2023 relative to publication; he does not give a precise Harvey rollout date. User counts and adoption observations are presented as current. His definition of power use is explicitly conditional on continued improvement: an advanced use case developed a year earlier is insufficient if the user stops developing it. Adoption is described in the context of prior training, organisational prioritisation, peer support and opportunities for experimentation. His advice to experiment relies on his characterisation of Harvey as a secure environment and on users understanding the technology sufficiently to design workflows. There is no dated future prediction.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected group is Repsol's corporate in-house legal team, with power users and champions helping colleagues change how they use AI.
pts.d: The account concerns the buyer-side legal department of an energy company, not a law firm's staffing or service-pricing model. Within its 150-user legal team, frequent users gain familiarity, qualitative power users pursue better output and new applications, and champions diffuse practices through pilots, training, shared use cases and informal conversations. Díez Tomillo identifies younger, technologically fluent and heavily loaded lawyers as more likely to become power users. Legal leadership, IT and other corporate functions support the organisational changes. The implied working model is lawyers using AI and designing workflows, rather than autonomous replacement of legal counsel. The source does not describe effects on external clients, access to justice, employment levels or the wider legal services market.
